THINK THROUGH THE RESULTS

Read it like a consultant

PFT report

Flagged: outside 80–120% of predicted (FEF 25–75% below 65%), FEV1/FVC below 0.70, or hemoglobin below 13 g/dL

INTERPRETATIONMake your own read first, then show the stepwise interpretation

    Course teaching rules: normal is 80–120% of predicted; FEV1/FVC below 0.70 is obstruction; a bronchodilator response is an FEV1 rise of at least 12% and 200 mL. Clinical labs use lower limits of normal from reference equations (ERS/ATS 2022).

    HOW THE TESTS WORK

    Spirometry

    The patient breathes through a flow sensor; volume is flow added up over time. Spirometry measures what moves in and out (tidal volume, IRV, ERV, vital capacity) but never the air that stays in the lungs, so RV, FRC, and TLC need another test.

    Why is forced expiration effort independent after roughly the first quarter of the vital capacity? As the patient pushes, pleural pressure squeezes the airways. At some point along each airway (the equal pressure point) the pressure inside equals the pressure outside, and downstream of it the airway is compressed. Pushing harder compresses it more, so flow stops rising. What is left to drive flow is the lung's own elastic recoil acting across the small airways upstream:

    V̇max = PL(V) / Rus

    That is why maximal flow falls as the lung empties (less recoil), why emphysema scoops the curve (less recoil and floppy airways), and why fibrosis can keep flows high for its volume (more recoil).

    Body box plethysmography

    Diffusing capacity (DLCO)

    The patient inhales a small amount of carbon monoxide with an inert tracer gas, holds for 10 seconds, and exhales. The analyzer measures how much CO disappeared; dilution of the tracer gives the alveolar volume it was spread through. CO has to cross the alveolar membrane and then bind hemoglobin, two steps in series, so their resistances add:

    1 / DLCO = 1 / DM + 1 / (θ · Vc)

    Emphysema destroys membrane and capillaries; fibrosis thickens the membrane; anemia lowers θ (less hemoglobin to bind CO), which is why the report also gives a hemoglobin-corrected value. Asthma and obesity spare the alveoli, so DLCO stays normal or high.

    Model details. Lung volumes come from the Statics page (lung, chest wall, and muscle curves). Forced expiratory flow is the smallest of three limits: PL/Rus, expiratory effort, and a central-airway maximum. Rus rises as lung recoil falls (small airways lose their tethering), and the airways close where Rus reaches ten times its open value. That closing volume sets RV when it is above the chest wall limit, which is how air trapping raises RV in emphysema. In a forced expiration the airways are also squeezed, so they close earlier (at seven times the open resistance); that is why SVC exceeds FVC in obstruction. DLCO assumes membrane and blood conductances in the ratio the ERS/ATS hemoglobin correction is built on, with a reference hemoglobin of 14.6 g/dL. The test ends when flow stays below 25 mL/s for 1 s (ERS/ATS 2019) or at 15 s. Not modeled: dynamic hyperinflation, the chest wall changes of aging, effort variability, gas dilution lung volumes, and the extra lung tissue volume of emphysema, so TLC rises less than in real patients.
